images.name: The cord tied thick, and what God unties
images.source: chain map: 4A. The Relation as Knot and Obligation; S13. An Oath Is Sworn, Thickened, and Released
images.scene: Two parties bind a cord between them with their right hands. It is twisted thick so it will not give, and one party holds its end. Only the one with authority can loosen a knot. A cord pulled wrongly becomes a stranglehold that keeps someone from what is theirs.

members.role: the cord or tie that fastens
the covenant confirmed by oath
the cord's thickness: something thin made stout
the oath made more stringent (taghlīẓ al-yamīn)
the women take hold of the cord's end
tying ends together into a knot
the pledge made binding
the right hand that ties
the oath sworn by the right hand
a bond of ownership held 'by the right hand'
the marriage contract as the knot
joining one thing to another, a fastening
a decree that is binding
untying a knot (denied: 'it is not untied for you')
the knot loosened by God
formal release of what an oath had bound
the wrongful squeeze that keeps someone from their right

images.containment: Aḥalla means God made lawful, and the word's root still pictures a knot being untied. Mīthāq ghalīẓ is a solemn covenant, and it is also a cord twisted thick whose end the women hold.
images.perceptible: The ayah asks 'how could you take it back?' because a man cannot pull his gift out of a knot he tied with his own hand and thickened, especially when the other party is holding it. Ḥalāl comes across as something loosened by the only hand that has authority over the knot, and ḥarām as what stays tied. ʿAḍl is the ugly reverse: the same cord pulled into a chokehold.

interactions.how: The knot and the joining are the two things that make a marriage: the tie (mīthāq) and the reaching (afḍā) sit side by side in 4:21, and neither stands in for the other.
Because the knot is tied, gifts that pass through it cannot be taken back; the cord is what makes 'taking' (akhdh) into buhtān.
Untying (ḥall) also names the ground outside the forbidden precinct (ḥill), so the knot scene and the enclosure scene meet in one root.
4:33's 'those your right hands tied' shows the knot producing a share (naṣīb).

images.movement: It turns a list of prohibitions and permissions into acts of tying and untying. The window's demand becomes this: keep the knot you tied, and do not use it to strangle.

images.name: Precinct, fortress, the ground beyond, and spilled water
images.source: chain map: 5A. Enclosure Against Uncontracted Spill; S12. Raised Plaster Makes a Fortress, Not an Escape from Death
images.scene: A map of rings. The innermost is a protected precinct (ḥarīm), like the zone around a well or a house, that no one may take for himself. Next is a fortress whose inside cannot be reached. Beyond these lies open ground (ḥill, warāʾ). There a man may seek, pay, and enter, building a fortress of his own. The alternative is pouring water out onto the ground with no vessel to hold it. Inside the fortress, the one who stays guards what is hidden while the husband is away, and God guards the walls.

members.role: the protected precinct around a place (ḥarīm of well or house)
the maḥārim, kin who fall within the precinct
the fortress whose interior cannot be reached
a woman already inside the fortress through a marriage bond
ḥill: the ground outside the precinct, where the ban lifts
the side beyond the rings
going out to seek on open ground
the man as builder of a fortress
keeping oneself chaste
liquid poured out and wasted
'pouring water without a contract' (maqāyīs), water lost to waste (jamhara)
the woman keeping herself chaste
a companion of desire kept hidden, a private door in the wall
brought inside a fortress by marriage
going inside
the one inside who watches over what is kept
the husband's absence, which the woman guards
God as the outer guard

images.containment: Married women are forbidden to you, and muḥṣanāt also shows them inside a fortress whose interior cannot be reached. Musāfiḥ means fornicator, and its root also pictures water poured onto the ground with no vessel to keep it.
images.perceptible: 4:23–25 read as a map with directions: inner precinct, fortress, the ground 'beyond that' (warāʾa dhālikum), and the choice between building a fortress (muḥṣinīn) and spilling water (musāfiḥīn). The contrast in 4:24 becomes physical: one act contains, the other pours away. Guarding 'for the unseen' in 4:34 finishes the picture: the fortress keeps its inside even when its master is gone, because God is guarding it (bi-mā ḥafiẓa Allāh).

interactions.how: The inner precinct is the kin circle drawn on the body; I3 fills in who stands in the innermost ring.
Ḥall is both untying and the ground outside the ḥaram; entering the fortress is done through the knot of nikāḥ.
Dakhaltum bihinna is entering the fortress; I4 is the joining that happens inside it.
Pouring out (sifāḥ) is also the arrow that draws no share: spilled water leaves nothing behind.
The fortress of 4:24–25 turns up again in 4:34 as the household guarded 'in absence'; nushūz is a disturbance inside those walls.

images.movement: It gives the legal middle of the window (4:23–25) a spatial logic the reader can walk through: boundaries are rings of protection around what is precious, not arbitrary bans.

images.name: Kinship drawn on the body: womb, milk, lap, spine
images.source: chain map: S11. Milk Flow Produces a Kinship Relation
images.scene: The forbidden list follows the body outward from the self. First the mothers you came from. Then those who come from you. Then those fed at the same breast, the stepdaughter carried in your lap, and the son who came from your back. The list ends on raḥīm, whose root also names the womb.

members.role: fatherhood as begetting and rearing
the mother who bore and reared you
the mother as origin, gathering point and place of return
those who issue from you
siblings sharing one origin
sucking milk from the breast
the milk bond that stands in for blood kinship
the stepchild raised in the household
tending and bringing to completion
the lap or bosom where a child is held
the lap as a protecting restraint
spouses as 'those who alight in one place'
the back and spine from which offspring come
kinship of the womb
the womb itself

images.containment: These women are forbidden to you in marriage, and the list's own words (milk, lap, loins, and the closing raḥīm) also trace a map of the body from which the prohibition grows.
images.perceptible: The prohibition follows bodily nearness: breast, lap and spine make kin just as birth does. Milk makes 'mothers' and 'sisters'. The stepdaughter 'in your laps' is a child you held. When the list closes on God as Raḥīm, the root of raḥim (womb) lets the reader hear that this nearness is protected by the One whose mercy carries the womb's name.

interactions.how: I3 is the innermost ring of I2's map of enclosures.
Joining (dakhaltum bihinna, 4:23) decides whether a stepdaughter enters the forbidden circle, so access redraws the kin map.

images.movement: It anchors the prohibitions in the body and in nurture, and prepares for the turn to God's mercy (ghafūr raḥīm) that closes 4:23.

images.name: Reaching all the way to the other, alighting together
images.source: chain map: 4B. The Relation as Access and Joining
images.scene: Two halves of one pair travel toward each other until each reaches the other with nothing left between them. They go in, share one lodging and one bed, and live mixed together. The window ends with God bringing the believers into a noble place of entry.

members.role: reaching the other and arriving at the end of the way
marital union
open space with nothing in between
one part of a whole
the other part
the counterpart joined to its match
bodily union
living intermixed
consummation as 'going in'
alighting and settling in one place
parts that come from one another
the shared bed
God bringing people in
the noble place of entry

images.containment: Afḍā baʿḍukum ilā baʿḍ means you went in to one another, and the verb also shows each reaching all the way to the other, arriving where nothing stands between.
images.perceptible: The argument in 4:21 is physical. You cannot claw back a gift after two parts of one whole have reached each other through open space with nothing between them. The 'going in' (dakhala) of 4:23 is echoed in 4:31 by God's 'bringing in' to a noble entrance, so human entry into intimacy is framed by a larger entry that God grants.

interactions.how: The knot (mīthāq) and the reaching (afḍā) are paired in 4:21 as the two reasons the gift is untouchable.
The shared bed of I4 is where 4:34's withdrawal (hajr fī al-maḍājiʿ) takes place: separation is measured against this joining.
Baʿḍ…ilā baʿḍ (toward) comes back as baʿḍ min baʿḍ (from) and baʿḍ ʿalā baʿḍ (over).

images.movement: It supplies the bodily and relational reason behind the property rules, and connects the married 'entering' to the promised entering of 4:31.

images.name: Given, notched and consented to, or seized and swallowed
images.source: chain map: 5B. Recognized Transfer Rather Than Seizure; 7A. Exchange With or Without a Valid Basis; S29. Set Work Generates an Owed Wage
images.scene: Property moves between people along one of two paths. On one path a gift is handed over, its measure cut into it like a notch, paid as a wage, spent on others, and exchanged by consent that runs both ways. On the other it is taken by force, carried off, snatched back, or eaten on a basis that has no substance.

members.role: ownership gained without contract or effort
forcing another against their will
walking off with part of the gift
the handing over
a heap of gold or silver
taking back into one's own hand
a stupefying wrong that leaves the onlooker speechless
a lie that dumbfounds
what is owed as a due
a notch cut into the thing
an obligation with a known limit
a gift measured and marked, given with no expectation of return
consent that runs both ways
consuming and seizing property
a basis that has left the truth and does not hold
trade seeking profit
mutual consent
wealth going out as spending on others

images.containment: The dower is a prescribed obligation (farīḍa), and the word also shows a measure cut into it like a notch, a marked gift given without expecting anything back.
images.perceptible: The window traces the direction property travels. Toward the woman: given, notched, owed, spent. Away from her: inherited as if she were property, carried off, taken back, eaten. The forms taraḍaytum and tarāḍin are both 'mutual', so consent is heard as something that passes both ways across the exchange. Buhtān is the kind of wrong that leaves the onlooker speechless.

interactions.how: The knot is what turns taking back into buhtān.
Eating on a void basis (akl bil-bāṭil) opens straight onto eating that feeds a fire.
The notch in farīḍa is the notch of a share-arrow; sifāḥ draws no notched share.
The husband's spending (anfaqū) in 4:34 is the gift's path continuing inside the household.

images.movement: It joins the marriage laws (4:19–25) to the general law of wealth (4:29) and the rules of shares (4:32–33). In every case, what is right is transfer by consent, not seizure.

images.name: Eating that feeds the fire
images.source: chain map: 7B. Appropriation as Self-Killing and Fire
images.scene: A community eats one another's property. In Arabic the same verb says a fire 'eats' its firewood, and the fire spreads until it reaches the eaters. Taking from others turns into killing oneself, and the blood shed goes unavenged and without compensation. The one who does it is made to meet the fire and is roasted by it.

members.role: feeding a fire, and the fire flaring up
the shared space between people where it happens
blood gone for nothing, with no revenge and no blood-money
taking a life
the living self
one's own self: 'yourselves' is 'one another'
overstepping the limit
putting a thing in the wrong place
withholding what is owed
being brought to meet the fire's heat
being held to the fire and roasted
the burning fire

images.containment: Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, and the verb 'eat' also carries the sense of a fire eating its fuel, so the one who eats this way is feeding the fire that 4:30 says will reach him.
images.perceptible: The cause and effect in 4:29–30 becomes one continuous physical process: eating wrongly is feeding a fire, and the fire turns back on the eater. 'Do not kill yourselves' sits right after 'do not eat your wealth among yourselves', and both use the same collective self. Harming another's property wounds the shared body the harmer belongs to, and bāṭil also calls to mind blood spilled with no redress.

interactions.how: I6 is where the seizure path of I5 ends up.
4:29 closes with God being 'merciful toward you', continuing the lightening of 4:28: forbidding self-destruction is a mercy to a weak creature.
The fire (4:30) and the noble entrance (4:31) are the two places one can be brought into.

images.movement: It carries the window from family property out to the whole community's wealth and gives the warning a bodily ending, before 4:31 opens the opposite entrance.

images.name: The trodden road and the great veer
images.source: chain map: 6A. Tilt Against Responsible Standing
images.scene: Travelers are led along a worn road that earlier travelers walked. Others, following the pull of appetite, want them to lean far off the road. Some leanings carry no blame (lā junāḥ). Some roads are bad roads. The great wrongs are to be skirted by keeping to one side of them. A husband is told not to look for a road against his wife.

members.role: a road that is traveled: 'an evil road'
leaning to one side
a lean toward wrong, here negated
gently guiding onto the way
the worn road, a way of life others followed
those who went ahead
walking behind
the pull of the self toward what it desires
turning off to one side
the veer itself
how great the veer is
going past the limit
stepping over and past
keeping to one side, apart from the great wrongs
staying upright and level
overreaching
a road opened against another person
veering off course to either side

images.containment: God wants to guide you in the ways (sunan) of those before you, and sunan also shows a worn road earlier travelers walked. Those who follow desires want you to veer, and mayl is literally a leaning off to one side.
images.perceptible: 4:26–27 sets two pulls against each other: God's gentle leading along a known road, and appetite's pull toward a great sideways lean. Lā junāḥ ('no blame') then sounds like 'no lean': permitted things do not tip you off the road. 'Seek no road against them' in 4:34 uses the same word as 'an evil road' in 4:22, so the household ruling becomes a question of which road a man opens.

interactions.how: The veer is dangerous because the traveler is weak (4:28), and God's answer is to lighten the load, not to tighten the rein.
Qawwām (standing upright) and shiqāq (veering to both sides) carry the road image into the household.
The great veer is also the spill outside the fortress: fāḥisha means going past the limit.

images.movement: It is the hinge of the window (4:26–28). The detailed laws turn out to be a road God clears, set against a pull away from it.

images.name: The weak frame: reach, a re-broken bone, a lightened load
images.source: chain map: S2. Obligation Scaled to Human Capacity
images.scene: A person created weak, with only so much reach and means, carries a load. There is a real danger that a bone already set will break again. Endurance holds the frame together, and God turns back toward the person, lightening the load and loosening what had been forbidden.

members.role: capacity to bear
means and power
length, how far one can reach
setting a broken bone (often healing crooked)
severe hardship that threatens ruin
a set bone breaking again
holding oneself back from giving way
God turning back to the servant
God turning people back toward lightness and permission (tahdhīb)
lightening the weight
shaping to a measure
lacking strength
a hardship borne unwillingly
ease after difficulty (for God, not for the wrongdoer)

images.containment: ʿAnat is grave hardship or falling into sin, and the word also names a healed bone that breaks again. The permission in 4:25 is for someone who fears exactly that.
images.perceptible: The concession in 4:25 is shaped around a fragile body. A man with too little reach (ṭawl) who fears a relapse-break (ʿanat) is given a way that fits his strength, while patience (ṣabr) is named as better. In 4:26–28 God's 'turning' (tawba) is explicitly a turning toward lightening (tahdhīb glosses tāba ʿalaykum as 'He brought you back to lightness'), because the creature is weak by make.

interactions.how: The weak traveler of I8 is the one the great veer (I7) threatens.
'Do not kill yourselves' protects the same weak frame, and God's being raḥīm continues the lightening.
The ajr of 4:25 is both a due and, in the coalition with ʿanat, something that sets what is broken.

images.movement: It explains why the law bends in 4:25 and why 4:26–28 speaks of God's will three times: the law is fitted to a creature that can break.

images.name: Standing, rising up, the split between, and the fitting
images.source: chain map: 6B. From Raised Resistance to Matched Mediation; 6A. Tilt Against Responsible Standing; S7. The Bow Is Tested, Nocked, and Drawn
images.scene: A household stands on those who hold it up and pay for it. One side rises up from its place (nushūz, literally raised ground). The bed that was shared becomes the place of withdrawal. The gap between the two opens into a split into two halves. Each family sends a person to settle it, and if repair is wanted God fits the two together, as a notch fits its string. Above all of it stands the One who alone is truly high.

members.role: care, protection and guardianship
the pillar and means of living that others rest on
standing upright
spending that keeps the household standing
humble devotion to God
long standing in prayer, the women's own standing
raised, jutting ground
getting up and leaving one's place
marital estrangement, which the dictionary says can come from either spouse
a sobering reminder that softens the heart
cutting contact, moving apart
the place where one lies down
going along, coming into agreement
overreaching against the other
true height
a crack opening
each party becoming its own half or side
a community breaking apart through dispute
the gap that separates
sending an envoy
the one the matter is entrusted to
holding back in order to set right
the circle of kin on each side
ending the estrangement
two things fitting and coming together
seating an arrow's notch on the bowstring
the link that joins the two sides

images.containment: Nushūz means a wife's ill-conduct toward the marriage, and the word also shows raised ground rising from its level. Shiqāq is discord, and the root pictures something cracked into two halves. Yuwaffiq means God grants reconciliation, and its root pictures two things fitting together.
images.perceptible: The steps in 4:34–35 read as a single physical sequence: something rises out of its place, the shared bed becomes the point of withdrawal, the gap between (bayn) cracks into two sides, and envoys are sent from both families so that God can fit the two back together. The same word bayn means both the gap and the link, and it appears twice: once as the split, once as what God repairs. Standing is shared: men stand for the household (qawwāmūn), women stand in devotion (qānitāt), and anyone who rises above the other is reminded that only God is 'Aliyy. The dictionary notes that nushūz can come from either spouse; the text addresses the case where the husbands fear it.

interactions.how: The shared bed and 'the between' of I4 are what this image puts at risk and then restores.
Shiqāq as veering, and the ban on seeking a road against her, tie the household to the road image.
The guarded interior (ḥāfiẓāt lil-ghayb) is what nushūz disturbs.
Arbitration works through the families (ahl) on both sides, the same families who gave permission in 4:25.

images.movement: It closes the window by turning the enclosures and knots into a living household that can crack and be mended. The last word belongs to God fitting the two together.

images.name: The notched share-arrow and the arrow that draws nothing
images.source: chain map: S6. Marked Arrows Divide the Slaughtered Camel
images.scene: A game of shares played with arrows. Some arrows carry notches marking how much they win (farḍ). One kind, the safīḥ, carries no share at all, and the classical lexicons extend its name to anyone whose work brings him nothing. The shares are raised and set aside for their owners. Against this game the window sets another rule: shares come from what each person earns, not from wishing for another's.

members.role: the arrow with no share; anyone whose deed yields nothing
the same, for women
the notch cut to mark a share
a fixed share set up for its owner
the share given to those bound by oath
a wish the heart pictures to itself
earning by seeking and obtaining
the surplus one share has over another
the arrow game that divides a slaughtered camel (faint echo)
al-nāfis, a share-arrow with five notches (faint echo)

images.containment: Musāfiḥ means one who fornicates without a contract, and the same word names the arrow in the old share game that wins nothing. Tahdhīb extends the name to anyone whose work brings him nothing.
images.perceptible: The contrast in 4:24 gains an economic edge: sifāḥ is unlawful and also unprofitable, since it produces no share, no notched due and no lineage. When 4:32 says 'men have a share of what they earned and women a share of what they earned', naṣīb means a portion that comes from kasb, not from wishful hoping (tamannī) for what was allotted to someone else.

interactions.how: The farīḍa's notch in I5 is the share-notch here.
Spilled water and the empty arrow are two sides of the same fruitlessness.
Faḍl as surplus is the difference between shares that 4:32 forbids coveting.

images.movement: It links the marriage laws to the rules of shares (4:32–33), so the reader hears both as a single fair allotment.

images.name: Parts of one whole: toward, from, over
images.scene: One body made of parts (baʿḍ) whose relation shifts with the preposition. They reach toward each other (ilā, 4:21), come from each other (min, 4:25), and some are given more than others (ʿalā, 4:32, 4:34). The surplus (faḍl) that distinguishes them comes from God, and people are told to ask Him for it.

members.role: part reaching toward part
part coming from part (free and slave of one origin)
part given more than another
part given more than another, within the household
degree and distinction
God's bounty and gift, open to anyone who asks
surplus or extra

images.containment: God has favored some of you over others, and the recurring baʿḍakum ʿalā baʿḍ also keeps both sides as parts of one whole, in the same phrasing that described them reaching toward and coming from each other.
images.perceptible: The reader sees that 4:32 and 4:34 do not say 'men over women' in so many words. They say 'some over some', using the same pair of parts that in 4:21 reached toward each other and in 4:25 came from each other. Whatever distinction exists is placed inside a single body, and its source is God's faḍl, which everyone may ask for.

interactions.how: It grows out of the baʿḍ…ilā baʿḍ of 4:21.
The 'over' of 4:34 is immediately limited by 'seek no road against them' and by God's being 'Aliyy.
Faḍl as the difference between shares.

images.movement: It keeps the hierarchy language of 4:32–34 tied to the mutuality language of 4:21–25.

concepts.concept: Untying so one can settle. Travelers untie their loads when they alight, so the same act gives 'untied, permitted' (ḥalāl, ḥill outside the ḥaram, release from an oath) and 'alighting together' (ḥalīla, a spouse). What God unties becomes a place where two people can live.
An enclosure whose interior cannot be reached: a fortress, chastity, and the protected state marriage gives are one idea applied to a person.

The between: the gap that separates, the middle space, the link across it, and the clarity that comes when something stands apart. Discord (shiqāq baynihimā) and repair (yuwaffiq baynahumā) both happen in it, and God's 'making clear' (li-yubayyina) is a case of it.
Standing upright as holding something up: bodily standing, care and guardianship, staying level, and being the pillar others live on.
A cut mark that fixes a measure: the notch, the obligation with a known limit, and the marked gift given without expecting return.
Desire going outward: lawful seeking (tabtaghū, 4:24), overreaching (tabghū, 4:34), and bighāʾ (fornication), all as one movement that either stays within a limit or goes past it.
Turning back: the servant returning to God, and God returning to the servant, which the tahdhīb reads for this passage as bringing people back to lightness and permission.
Consent as something that passes between parties: plain contentment, and consent that runs both ways (tarāḍī), which is what makes an exchange lawful.
What is more: surplus, rank, and gift. God's distinguishing some over others and His bounty that anyone may ask for are one faḍl.
Rising out of one's level: raised ground, getting up and leaving one's seat, and a spouse rising against the marriage.
Splitting into halves: a crack, each half becoming a side, a community falling apart, and veering to either side.

movement: The window begins with women treated as property that can be inherited, squeezed and carried off (4:19–20). It answers with two reasons the woman's gift cannot be touched: the partners have reached each other with nothing left between them, and they are tied by a cord the women hold, twisted thick (4:21; I4, I1). Next it maps the ground of lawful intimacy as rings: kin drawn on the body (womb, milk, lap, spine), married women inside a fortress, and open ground beyond. On that open ground a man seeks with his wealth and builds a fortress of his own instead of pouring water that yields no share (4:22–25; I3, I2, I10). For a weak man who fears a relapse-break, the law bends (4:25; I8). At the hinge (4:26–28) God's will is stated three times, to make clear, to guide along a worn road, and to turn toward and lighten, against appetite's pull toward a great veer, because the human being is made weak (I7, I8). The same logic then covers all wealth: transfer by mutual consent, never eating that feeds a fire and becomes self-killing (4:29–30; I5, I6), with a noble entrance opened to anyone who skirts the great wrongs (4:31; I4). Shares come from earning and from God's bounty, not from wishing (4:32–33; I10, I11). Finally the household itself: it stands on those who hold it up and spend, is guarded inside when the husband is away, may crack when one side rises up, and is mended when envoys from both families are sent and God fits the two together (4:34–35; I9, I2). Throughout, a relationship is held by binding, protection and consent, never by force, and God is the one who unties, guards, lightens and fits.

plan.note: Show the scene of women inherited 'by force' like goods, and the wrongful squeeze of ʿaḍl (I1: a cord pulled into a chokehold, the opposite of a bond). 'Walking off with part of what you gave' opens the path of property (I5). Treat ʿāshirūhunna as living mixed together (I4). Mention briefly that karh is also a burden borne (I8), and keep the plain promise that God may place much good in what is disliked.
A heap of gold handed over, then taken back. Buhtān as a wrong that leaves the onlooker speechless. Istibdāl (one wife put 'in the place' of another) shows the danger of treating a person as a slot.

This is the central image of the first part. Afḍā: each reached all the way to the other, arriving where nothing stands between. Mīthāq ghalīẓ: a cord twisted thick, with its end in the women's hands. Both reasons together make 'how could you take it?' unanswerable. Introduce baʿḍ ilā baʿḍ as parts of one whole.
Nikāḥ as both knot and union. The father's wife as the first ring of the forbidden. 'An evil road' starts the road image (I7). Maqt is the plain sense, and the old name nikāḥ al-maqt belongs here.

Present the list as a map of the body: mothers as origin, milk that makes kin, the stepdaughter held in the lap, sons from the back, and the list closing on raḥīm, whose root names the womb. Ḥurrimat as the protected precinct (ḥarīm) around a well or house, the innermost ring. Dakhaltum bihinna, going in, decides whether the stepdaughter enters the circle. Lā junāḥ as 'no lean' is mentioned only briefly here.

The spatial hinge: the fortress of married women, then uḥilla (the ḥill, ground outside the precinct and a knot untied) 'beyond that' (warāʾ). Seeking with wealth as fortress-builders (muḥṣinīn), not pourers of water (musāfiḥīn: water poured without a contract). The farīḍa as a notched, marked gift, and mutual consent. Point out lightly that the safīḥ is also the arrow that wins nothing.

Too little reach (ṭawl) and the fear of ʿanat, a set bone breaking again, shape the concession, with ṣabr named as better. The families' permission, the ajr paid 'in the recognized way'. Hidden companions (akhdān) as a secret door in the fortress wall. 'You are from one another' places free and slave inside one whole (I11).

God's threefold will. Make clear (the between becomes visible), guide along the worn road of those who went before (sunan), and turn toward you. Keep the plain sense: the ways of earlier righteous people.
Two wills pull against each other: God's turning toward you, and those following appetite who want a great sideways lean (mayl ʿaẓīm). The road image reaches its climax here.

Lightening a load for a frame made weak. The tahdhīb reads God's tawba here as a return to lightness and permission, which ties the three verbs together. This is where the reason behind the whole law becomes clear.

'Eating' wealth, and the same verb for fire eating fuel. A void basis (bāṭil) set against trade by mutual consent. 'Do not kill yourselves' uses the collective self: to harm another is to wound the body one belongs to. God's mercy continues the lightening of 4:28.
Overstepping and misplacing lead to being brought to the fire and roasted. The fire that eating fed now reaches the eater. 'Easy for God' names an ease that belongs to God alone.

Keep to one side of the great wrongs (ijtināb). God covers the lesser misdeeds and brings you into a noble place of entry. This entering answers the human 'going in' of 4:23 and stands opposite the fire of 4:30.

'Some over some', not 'men over women' in so many words. Do not picture to yourself (tamannī) the share allotted to another. Each has a share that stands for what they earned. Ask God for His bounty (faḍl), which has no fixed notch.
The mawālī (heirs and close ones) of what parents and relatives leave. 'Those your right hands tied': the knot produces a share to be handed over. God witnesses all of it.

Standing as holding up and spending (qawwāmūn), against the women's own standing in devotion (qānitāt). The fortress guarded in the husband's absence while God guards the wall. Nushūz as raised ground rising from its level. The shared bed turned into the place of withdrawal. 'Seek no road against them.' Only God is 'Aliyy, 'Kabīr'. Do not force any latent branch onto iḍribūhunna; give its plain sense and let the image work through the structure of the verse and its limits.

Shiqāq: the gap between cracks into two halves. Envoys are sent from each family. If they want repair, God fits the two together, as a notch fits its string. Bayn appears twice, as the split and as what God repairs. Ending on 'Knowing, Aware' of what lies inside.

chains_set_aside.title: S8. A Timed Watering Turn Makes Room for the Thirsty Animal
chains_set_aside.why: In this window its only anchors are salafa ('what has passed') and dakhala, both fully used in their plain or marital senses. No word here supplies the herd, the water or the drinking, so the scene would only add noise.

chains_set_aside.title: S10. Prepared Drink Moves from Mixture to Lost Sobriety
chains_set_aside.why: Its window member is qatl in the sense of diluting wine with water. 4:29's 'do not kill yourselves' is fully carried by I6 (self-killing and fire), and nothing nearby activates the drink.

chains_set_aside.title: S14. The Final Breath Is Enclosed in a Grave-House
chains_set_aside.why: The only local member is ghayb (burial). In 4:34 al-ghayb is the husband's absence (B005), which I2 uses. A grave reading would work against the image of a guarded household.

chains_set_aside.title: S17. A Debt Follows Claim, Surety, Payment, and Discharge
chains_set_aside.why: Tabiʿa as the creditor's pursuit (4:27 yattabiʿūn) is overshadowed by following on a road (I7). The debt scene has no other members here.

chains_set_aside.title: S23. Fire Assays Gold While Gilding Imitates It
chains_set_aside.why: Dhahab/qinṭār (gold) in 4:19–20 is noted as an activation, but there is no assaying or imitation in this window. The gold sits inside I5's scene of transfer.

chains_set_aside.title: S25. A Pot on Three Stones Is Brought to Doneness
chains_set_aside.why: Jaʿala as the cloth used to lift a pot has nothing in 4:19 or 4:33 to activate it.

chains_set_aside.title: S28. A Forward Sale Begins with Appraisal and Known Price
chains_set_aside.why: Salaf as money paid in advance and qawwām as valuation have no support: 'illā mā qad salaf' is clearly temporal, and qawwāmūn is carried by care and standing (I9).

chains_set_aside.title: S7. The Bow Is Tested, Nocked, and Drawn
chains_set_aside.why: Kept only in one member: wafq B006 (seating the notch on the string) enters I9 as the fitting. The archery scene as a whole (ʿanat as a bow, bayn as a bow gap) adds nothing here.

chains_set_aside.title: S12. Raised Plaster Makes a Fortress, Not an Escape from Death
chains_set_aside.why: Only the fortress element (ḥiṣn B001) is kept, inside I2. Towers, plaster and death belong to 4:78 and play no part in this window.

other_activations: 4:19:12 ع ض ل B005 (a child or egg stuck, unable to come out): activated by the confinement in karhan and 'to go off with'. The woman held back from a new marriage is like a birth that cannot happen. Not built into an image; could be mentioned beside I1's chokehold.
4:19:13 ذ ه ب B001 (gold): activated by qinṭār (a heap of gold) in 4:20. 'To go off with' is heard next to the gold being carried off.
4:19:10 ك ر ه B007 (hard, rough ground), with 4:19:26 ع س ي B002 (hardness) and 4:19:33–34 خ ي ر / ك ث ر: ground one dislikes that God makes yield much good. Only a faint scene.
4:23:5 ء خ و B002 (ākhiyya, a tether loop): activated by the cord scene of mīthāq and ʿaqadat (I1). Kin are heard faintly as a tether.

4:34:26 ه ج ر B007 (tying with a hijār rope): attested in the dictionary and known from a classical tafsir discussion of this verse. Deliberately not built into any image, to avoid pressing an unsupported sense onto a sensitive ruling.
4:25:41 ن ص ف B006 (naṣīf, a veil that screens a woman from view): activated by the muḥṣanāt around it. Niṣf stays 'half' in the plain sense.
4:22:15 م ق ت B002 (nikāḥ al-maqt): the pre-Islamic name for marrying a father's widow, which the word maqt here directly recalls.
4:20:3 ب د ل B001 with 4:20:5 ك و ن B002 (place): one wife put 'in the place' of another, as if a person were a replaceable slot.

4:31:7 ك ف ر B001/B009 (covering, erasing sin by covering it), with 4:23:53 and 4:25:57 غ ف ر B001 (a cover that protects): God's covering gestures sit next to the fortress image but are not joined to it.
4:33:3 و ل ي B001 (nearness with nothing in between): mawālī are those who stand closest, echoing afḍā's 'nothing between'.
4:24:23 م ت ع B005 (the enjoyment of marriage, and the temporary marriage called mutʿa): the plain legal debate over this word is noted; no latent image is built on it.
